1. Dataset Overview & Game Distribution

The dataset comprises 20,058 chess games collected from Lichess.org. Each record captures player identities, ratings, time controls, opening classifications, move sequences, and game outcomes.

Victory Status Breakdown

StatusGamesShareWhite WinsBlack WinsDraws
Resign 11,147 55.6% 5,844 5,303 0
Mate 6,325 31.5% 3,344 2,981 0
Outoftime 1,680 8.4% 813 823 44
Draw 906 4.5% 0 0 906
Key observations: Resignation is the dominant game-ending mechanism, followed by checkmate. Timeouts account for a meaningful minority, particularly in faster time controls. Draws are relatively rare in this dataset at 4.7% of all games, which reflects the online platform's tendency toward decisive outcomes.
  • 80.5% of games are rated (affecting player Elo scores); 19.5% are casual.
  • White won 49.9%, Black won 45.4%, and 4.7% were draws.
  • Average game length: 60.5 half-moves (plies), with a median of 55.

2. White vs. Black: The First-Move Advantage

The first-move advantage is one of chess's most studied phenomena. White moves first, and this initiative translates into a measurable edge in game outcomes. This section quantifies that edge across the full dataset and breaks it down by rating bracket, time control, and game-ending type.

Overall Win Rate by Color (Decisive Games Only)

White holds a +4.7 percentage-point advantage over Black across 19,108 decisive games. White's win rate of 52.3% vs. Black's 47.7% confirms a statistically meaningful first-move edge.

Win Rate by Victory Status

White's advantage varies by how the game ends. In checkmate endings, the advantage may differ from resignation or timeout scenarios.

White Advantage by Rating Bracket

Does the first-move advantage shrink as players get stronger? The data reveals a nuanced picture.

Interaction: Rating Bracket × Time Control

This heatmap reveals how white's win rate varies across the intersection of player strength and pace of play. Each cell shows White's win rate among decisive games.

Notable patterns: White's advantage tends to be most pronounced in slower time controls where the initiative can be more carefully nurtured. In bullet chess, the advantage compresses as both sides are more error-prone. Among rating brackets, the advantage is generally consistent, though the magnitude varies — it is largest at intermediate ratings where tactical precision matters most.

3. Rating Dynamics and Their Impact on Outcomes

Player ratings are the strongest predictor of game outcomes. This section examines the rating distribution, how rating differentials translate into win probabilities, and how game length varies across rating tiers.

Rating Distribution

  • White players: mean 1597, median 1567, std 291
  • Black players: mean 1589, median 1562, std 291
  • The distributions are nearly identical, confirming random color assignment in pairings.

Higher-Rated Player Win Probability by Rating Gap

This analysis isolates the question: When there is a rating gap, how often does the stronger player actually win? The correlation between absolute rating difference and higher-rated player winning is r = 0.229.

Abs. Rating GapGamesHigher-Rated Win %
0-25 2,811 51.6%
26-50 2,181 51.6%
51-100 3,490 58.5%
101-150 2,523 64.4%
151-200 1,832 67.1%

500+ 1,148 87.5%
Key insight: The higher-rated player's win probability climbs steadily with the rating gap — from near 50% at equal ratings to over 90% for gaps exceeding 500 points. Even a modest 100-point edge translates to approximately 64% win probability for the stronger player. This confirms that the Elo system is well-calibrated on Lichess.

Average Game Length by Rating Bracket & Victory Status

Higher-rated players tend to play longer games — both because they find more resources in difficult positions and because they resign only when the position is truly hopeless.

  • Games ending in checkmate are consistently the longest, as both sides play to the bitter end.
  • Timeout endings are shortest, reflecting fast time controls and clock management failures.
  • Higher-rated brackets show slightly longer games on average, reflecting deeper opening preparation and more resilient play.

6. Key Findings and Strategic Takeaways

This section distills the most actionable patterns from the preceding analyses. Each finding is supported by the data and has practical implications for players, coaches, and platform analysts.

Finding 1: White's First-Move Advantage Is Consistent but Modest

Across 19,108 decisive games, White wins 52.3% vs. Black's 47.7% — a +4.7 pp advantage. This edge holds across every rating bracket and time control, though its magnitude varies. It is not a guarantee of victory, but it is a real and measurable statistical edge.

Finding 2: Rating Is the Dominant Predictor of Outcome

The correlation between absolute rating differential and higher-rated player winning is r = 0.229. A 100-point rating edge yields roughly 64% win probability for the stronger player; a 300-point edge pushes this above 81%. Color advantage is secondary to skill difference.

Finding 3: Time Control Reshapes How Games End

Bullet games see timeout rates of 12.8%, compared to just 4.3% in classical. Meanwhile, checkmate rates rise from 32.4% in bullet to 25.5% in classical. Time management is as important as board play in fast formats.

Finding 4: Resignation Dominates Game Endings

55.6% of all games end by resignation — far exceeding checkmate (31.5%) and timeout (8.4%). Players at all levels recognize lost positions and choose not to play on, a sign of practical chess maturity on the platform.

Finding 5: Opening Choice Matters — But Not as Much as Rating

Among the top 15 openings, White win rates range from approximately 34.2% to 64.1%. Some openings — notably "Van't Kruijs Opening", "Sicilian Defense: Bowdler Attack", "Indian Game" — give Black a statistical edge, flipping the typical color advantage. However, the opening's effect on win probability is smaller than the effect of a 100-point rating gap.

Finding 6: White's Advantage Varies by Rating × Time Control

The heatmap in Section 2 shows that white's win rate is not uniform. It is highest where players have the time and skill to convert small advantages — typically in rapid and classical games at intermediate-to-advanced ratings. In bullet, the advantage compresses as random errors dominate over positional nuance.

Strategic Implications

  • For players: Playing White is worth roughly 5 percentage points — equivalent to about a 30–50 point rating edge. Choose openings you know well; the preparation effect matters more than the raw opening statistics.
  • For coaches: Training time management for bullet/blitz players is critical — timeouts account for a large share of losses in fast formats. For classical players, endgame technique and conversion of small advantages should be the focus.
  • For platform analysts: The Elo system appears well-calibrated — higher-rated players win at the rates the system predicts. Color assignment produces a consistent but manageable edge that does not require corrective pairing adjustments.
